one_liner: Rust port of Seth Hillbrand's C++ stepreduce STEP CAD deduplicator; 5.2x faster than the std::regex C++ version, which has since caught up.
what_it_does: Shrinks ISO 10303-21 (STEP) CAD files by merging duplicate entities, then dropping entities that are unreachable from a fixed list of root entity types and renumbering the #ids. The library is one in-memory call, reduce(&[u8], &ReduceOptions) -> Vec<u8>, with optional rounding to N decimals or to the file's UNCERTAINTY_MEASURE_WITH_UNIT precision for comparisons. An optional CLI (feature cli, on by default) takes input and output paths like the C++ tool. It was written for LibrePCB's STEP minification.
how_it_is_fast: Same passes as the C++ original: repeated deduplication until a fixpoint, keyed on the entity text with numbers normalised and names blanked, followed by a reachability walk from root entity types. The 3.5x first step came from swapping libstdc++ std::regex for the Rust regex crate (lazy DFA) on the number, name and #ref patterns. A further 1.5x came from a hand-written float-literal scanner in place of the NUM_PATTERN regex, plus preallocating the dedup HashMaps. The repo has no profile, so the attribution is the author's.
when_to_use: Embedding STEP size reduction in a Rust application (the LibrePCB use case) without the C++ toolchain; the C++ CMake build has required OpenCASCADE since 2026-02-15 (for its --check verification).
Batch-minifying machine-generated STEP models (for example, component libraries) that repeat identical geometry entities, where file size matters more than keeping entity names.
When you want the CDSR and SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP root fixes, which keep assembly placements; C++ master has the first but not the second.
Projects that can accept GPL-3.0-or-later code.
when_not_to_use: Speed alone: the README's own 2026-02-25 update says the C++ project is slightly faster again, and the author put it at about 4% on his test file (LibrePCB issue #1693).
Files with non-UTF-8 bytes (for example, Latin-1 names written raw by some exporters): parsing stops silently at the first invalid line.
Workflows that must keep every entity name or exact metadata: names are left out of the dedup key, and the -p and --use-step-precision options merge entities whose numbers differ beyond N decimals.
Untrusted input on shared services: a '#' followed by more digits than fit in u32 panics, and a huge exponent such as 1E2000000000 makes normalize_number allocate gigabytes of '0' characters.
Critical CAD pipelines without your own validation: it is an LLM-assisted port with 0 stars and no crates.io release, and the author disclaims correctness beyond the test suite.

integration.dependencies: regex; clap and anyhow for the optional CLI
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 with let-chains in lib.rs and normalize.rs, so Rust 1.88 or later in practice (no rust-version declared)
integration.platforms: any Rust target (pure Rust, no unsafe or platform code in src/)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; reduce() is a pure function whose only statics are LazyLock<Regex>, so concurrent calls on separate inputs share no mutable state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the CLI takes the same input/output arguments, but output now differs from C++ master: Rust adds SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP as a GC root and types complex '( ... )' entities by their first member, where C++ returns an empty type

gotchas: Silent truncation: parse.rs iterates BufRead::lines() and breaks on the first Err. A single non-UTF-8 byte (checked with a std-only test: a Latin-1 'ü' stopped a 9-line file after line 4) drops the rest of DATA and the whole footer, with no error returned. The CLI allows output to be the input path, so it can overwrite the original with a broken file.

Orphan removal is a heuristic list of root types, and it has already lost geometry in real files twice: assembly placements were dropped until CDSR became a root (2026-02-15), and a proprietary model vanished in FreeCAD until SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP was added (2026-03-01). The C++ original had the same bugs, and the benchmarked 2026-02-14 Rust builds predate both fixes. The author has proposed switching to an allow-list of collectable types.

remap_references calls parse::<u32>().unwrap() on every '#\d+' match, including text inside quoted strings. A string such as '#12345678901' (u32 overflow) panics, as can non-ASCII digits, since the regex \d is Unicode-aware. The same pass rewrites '#N' inside string literals, a behaviour inherited from the C++ REF_PATTERN.

Harness: bench/ binaries and build commands are not committed, the C++ build type is unstated (issue #3 only asks whether CMake Release is right), and the run used one 1 MiB file. The 5.2x measured libstdc++ std::regex against the regex crate, not language codegen; both sides were 2026-02 builds that later received correctness fixes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling handles STEP files; the real alternative is the C++ original (GitLab sethhillbrand/stepreduce), now about 4% faster per the Rust author, with built-in --check geometric verification through OpenCASCADE. Pick the Rust port for Rust embedding, a build without OpenCASCADE and the extra SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP root fix, not for speed.
verified_claims_summary: One hyperfine run (3 warmups) on a 1 MiB STEP file on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X: the C++ stepreduce 2026-02-05 rewrite, which matched numbers, names and #refs with libstdc++ std::regex, took 505.4 ms, the first Rust port 145.2 ms, and the Rust build with a hand-written float scanner and preallocated maps 97.2 ms (5.20 +/- 0.10x); compiler versions and flags are not stated for either side. After C++ replaced its regexes on 2026-02-15, the Rust author reports the C++ about 4% faster (no published numbers), so the speed claim is obsolete.
status_note: Small single-author port (19 commits, last 2026-03-01, 0 stars, GPL-3.0-or-later, not published on crates.io; issue #2 is open), under evaluation for LibrePCB 2.2.0 (issue #1693 open). Its headline 5.2x is now reversed (C++ about 4% faster), it silently truncates non-UTF-8 input, and its orphan-removal heuristic has needed two geometry-loss fixes since the benchmark.
